MN202611_w7ubpumx0w.t:
Reports reaching Taarifa Congo Desk indicate that DRC troops have staged a counterattack and pushed back CRP rebels who recently overrun DRC Army Push Back Thomas Lubanga Fighters Retake Iga-Barrière in Djugu, Ituri.

Emerging reports indicate that FARDC have retaken control of; Iga-Barrière, Lopa and Lindji, located on National Road No. 27 in the territory of Djugu (Ituri).

According to the Congolese army, dislodging the Rebels followed Thursday’s fierce clashes with the fighters under the armed movement commanded by Thomas Lubanga also considered to be aligning with the FRN rebel group.

Meanwhile, during the brief rebel control of these areas, many residents had fled while economic activities got paralysed and traffic disruptions on National Route 27 (RN 27) for nearly five days.

The rebels had reinforced their positions considering fighting all the way to capture Bunia city about 25kms. However, their leader Thomas Lubanga had instructed them to halt the advance.

Despite the dislodgement of CRP rebels, Shops, stores, and markets remain closed in the Lopa and Iga-Barrière shopping centers.

The fighting has left fifteen CRP fighters reportedly killed while three FARDC soldiers were wounded.

A large part of the population has left these areas to flee the fighting, and many residents are still hesitant to return home due to persistent fears of renewed clashes.

MN202611_wabve14ruv.t:
Nyuma yo kuba mu bantu batatu dosiye zabo zitemewe mu bazokwitoza mu matora y'umukuru w'igihugu, Agathon Rwasa avuga ko agiye kwitura sentare yubahiriza ibwirizwa shingiro.

Pamphile Malayika, uwari yaserukiye Rwasa mu birori vy'umugwi ujejwe amatora CENI vyo gutangaza ivyavuye mu mwihwezo w'amadosiye y'abantu 10, yagize ati:

"Mw'ibwirizwa shingiro ryo muri 2018 ingingo ya 99 agace ka gatatu kagira gati 'Uwuri mu barongoye umugambwe ashobora kwitoza ku giti ciwe ari uko harangiye imyaka ibiri akuwe muri ayo mabanga canke atanze imihoho mu mugambwe yari arimwo".

Ku bwiwe kuba Rwasa yarakuwe ku burongonzi bw'umugabwe ivyo vyonyene birakwiye ko yemererwa kwitoza nk'uwigenga. CENI yo yasiguye ko uwushaka kwitoza nk'uwigenga ategerezwa gutanga urupapuro rwerekana ko amaze imyaka ibiri ata mugambwe n'umwe arimwo.

Rwasa ntarakurwa mu mugambwe CNL kandi ntaratangaza ko yawukuwemwo. Gusa yakuwe ku burongozi bwawo mu 2024.

Pamphile Malayika amenyesha ko bagiye kwitura sentare yubahiriza ibwirizwa shingiro kuko "amategeko arekurako ko uwutashimishijwe n'ingingo ya CENI ashobora kwitura sentare yubahiriza ibwirizwa shingiro".

Naho aticizere kinini afise, Malayika avuga ko "kumbure iyo sentare ishobora kumutunganiriza".

Abandi babiri amadosiye yabo atemewe – Valentin Kavakure yatanzwe n'umugambwe FPN Imboneza n'uwigenga Aloys Kamenyero yashaka kugarukana ubwami mu Burundi – bavuye mu birori bitarahera bagenda ataco bavuze.

Ayo matora y'umukuru w'igihugu azoba mu kwezi kwa gatanu 2027.

MN202611_1jdlrbfens9.t:
An official holds one of the seized Vallarta mud turtles - they are now receiving care at a specialised sanctuary

Twenty-six "very rare" turtles have been seized from a traveller's checked baggage at Amsterdam's Schiphol airport, a Dutch government agency has said.

The Netherlands Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority (NVWA) said a man flying from Mexico to Hong Kong via the airport was arrested on Saturday after the Vallarta mud turtles were found by customs officers.

The endangered species, thought to be the smallest freshwater turtles in the world with a maximum length of about 10cm (4in), were wrapped in duct tape to prevent them from moving.

The NVWA said they were "presumably stolen" from the wild in their native Mexico.

It said most of the turtles were found in a box with a toy car, while the others were in a closed sock inside a suitcase.

The arrested man remains in custody and an investigation is under way.

Meanwhile, the turtles are receiving care at a "specialised sanctuary", the NVWA said.

In 2025, the US NGO Turtle Island estimated that no more than 300 Vallarta mud turtles existed in the wild.

They are listed as critically endangered on a list published by the International Union for Conservation of Nature.

According to environmental news outlet Mongabay, a Vallarta mud turtle can sell for $10,000 (£7,500) or more on the black market in Asia.

Other cases of live turtles being smuggled to Hong Kong have been reported this year.

In October, customs authorities in Hong Kong were reported to have seized eight turtles , external that were thought to be endangered. The reptiles had an estimated market value of about $54,000.

Three months prior, Hong Kong customs detected two separate smuggling cases , external . Some 42 live turtles, with a total estimated market value of $210,000 were seized.

MN202611_f1jqj6fpww.t:
Colwill has one goal and three assists from 10 Championship appearances following Cardiff City's return to the Championship

Rubin Colwill is used to being in the centre of things.

He has been the focus of an ongoing argument over his role - or lack of it - in Craig Bellamy's Wales side.

It has meant the midfielder has been the subject of countless questions around international weeks, the latest prompting the Wales boss to ask a journalist if he had a Colwill poster in the middle of his bedroom wall.

The debate has stemmed from the 24-year-old being at the heart of Brian Barry-Murphy's stylish transformation of Cardiff City.

So it is understandable that, as he prepares to lead his boyhood club into the eye of the storm that is the south Wales derby, he is again in the centre of things.

And fitting for someone who grew up in the middle of the rivalry between the two cities.

"I took a lot of stick," Colwill said. Well, we presume that is what he might have said, stopping himself from swearing to describe life as a Cardiff fan from the town of Neath, nine miles from Swansea.

"I probably felt it more than most being surrounded by Swansea fans and a lot of mates being Swansea fans.

"It was tough because they were in the Premier League for a long spell, so I was always trying to give a bit back when we won a game or did well."

Bellamy an influence as Williams leads Swansea

Bellamy jokes reporter has Colwill poster in bedroom

Latest Cardiff City news, analysis and fan views

Colwill was always Cardiff, as was brother Joel, his team-mate for club and country.

Their mother - from Port Talbot, a little further east with a denser amount of support that turn towards the capital - was a Cardiff fan and so were her boys, signing for the club while still in primary school.

He has never gone to a derby in Swansea as a fan - he was never allowed - but was part of the Cardiff side that last won at their rivals in 2021 and has told team-mates all about the journey down the M4, where fans flock to bridges and encouragement turns to abuse as the miles clock up.

He will mention that, and the feeling of the times where, by his own admission, Cardiff were not good enough in a string of defeats that sting more than most.

But he will also share the "no better" feeling of being in the middle of the celebrations of a derby win, as he was in January 2025.

Colwill: 'Tough' growing up as a Cardiff fan

That Cardiff 3-0 victory was a rare high point in a season that eventually saw the club relegated from the Championship and in desperate need of a rebuild.

They have done just that, transitioning into an eye-catching, exciting team, who - depsite failing to win away this season and going into the game on the back of a 4-0 defeat by Preston North End - are ready to show Swansea the Bluebirds are a different beast these days.

Colwill and his influence has been very much a central cog in that change.

He has been game time and responsibility by Barry-Murphy - including the armband that might not be obvious for such a seemingly laidback character.

The academy product says he has learned much from the journey, including a frustrating spell of injuries that have limited his impact to seven starts since the return to the Championship.

It has seemingly been noticed by Bellamy, who spoke before Wales' recent Nations League defeat to Portugal about how he has improved as a player.

"There has been a big change in his game," Bellamy said, a former academy coach of the talented midfielder.

"He is a player I really like watching - before I did and I didn't. Now I see a lot of good things."

Colwill responded with a man-of-the-match performance against Portugal in what was his first competitive Wales start in five years.

"It was almost like I got to experience my first game twice," smiled Colwill.

Bellamy - who has questioned Colwill's work off the ball - has said he felt able to be more "ruthless" with the youngster because of their long association.

"Everyone knows," said Bellamy of what he thought Colwill needed to do to improve. "And none more than him."

Williams to lead Swansea in south Wales derby

Frozen out Robinson told he has Cardiff future

Despite being in the middle of it all, Colwill has not changed in playing personality, and certainly showed no pressure when he reclaimed his Wales spot.

Clearly there is a resilience that goes beyond sticking with a Cardiff scarf in an area full of Swansea colours.

"I've tried to learn from those experiences and develop myself mentally and improve my resilience so I can almost take anything that comes my way," he says.

"I think that's a massive part of football: you've got to stay grounded, stay focused, regardless if you're doing really well or really badly because it's a massive part of the game to stay consistent in the end."

So what of the challenge to improve and being in the middle of the two different approaches to getting the most out of him?

"I think they're very similar," is Colwill's response. "They both want to control the game, the structure, the body shape, how they want us to play, the press and reaction to giving the ball away.

"In the fundamentals of the game, they're similar. Obviously they're both different people so the approaches to that are very different, and it's in the little details.

"With Craig, he's always had that approach of if he thinks you can offer something or improve on, it's on us to take it on board and be open to that constructive criticism.

"It's not always easy. I think he does have a high demand of you, but if you do make a change as he asks of you then he will play you."

Cardiff players will have 'edge' against Swansea

After the stick, the carrot at Cardiff is the chance to follow in Bellamy's footsteps by scoring a winner in the derby at Swansea, as the Wales boss did in 2011 - Cardiff's last win there in front of travelling supporters.

Colwill smiles at the thought, just as he winces at the memories of the defeats - as a player and a fan - which is why he will not be telling team-mates to treat this game like just another.

"That attitude is almost like trying to protect yourself from the pressure," he argues. "But it's not. We have a lot of boys from the area who have come from the academy who really get the game and understand the whole picture of it and how important it is for everyone in the city.

"And we've got no fear of failure - if we lose we just leave it all out there, but we have full belief we can win."

If they do, it will come as no surprise if Colwill is at the heart of it.

MN202611_11em6rff389.t:
Houthis said they were responsible for an attack on an oil facility south of Riyadh on 3 October, one of a growing number

Ten days after fleeing his home in Yemen's capital, Sanaa, Abu Khalil is selling socks on the streets of Riyadh.

"I walked out of Sanaa, I crossed the front line," he says, adding that he "hitched a ride into Saudi Arabia".

Families in Yemen are "struggling to provide for [their] children", he says, as he tries to earn enough to send some money home.

He asks us not to use his full name because his wife and four children are still in Sanaa, and he is frightened of what might happen to them if he is identified speaking out against the Houthis. "I ran away from the Houthis but I couldn't bring my family with me. May God protect them," he says.

Backed by Iran, the armed group has controlled much of northern Yemen since a civil war erupted more than a decade ago. It is fighting the internationally recognised government, which is supported by neighbouring Saudi Arabia.

And Saudi cities, such as Riyadh, are now coming under regular drone and missile attacks from the very group Abu Khalil fled.

An informal ceasefire in Yemen unravelled in July, and since the fighting escalated, the Houthis have stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia. They have said they were retaliating against deadly Saudi air strikes in Yemen and what they say is a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in Houthi-controlled territory.

One Houthi strike on Riyadh's international airport on 10 October killed 13 people and injured more than 300 - the deadliest attack on Saudi soil in years.

Surveillance footage shows the moment of the attack at King Khalid International Airport on 10 October

Having been granted rare permission to report from Riyadh, we spoke to locals, including Majid, a 25-year-old engineer who works for the Saudi state oil company Aramco. He was passing through the airport that day, rushing for a flight to Jeddah for a religious pilgrimage.

He says he was watching a mother push her children in a pushchair when the terminal was hit.

He remembers seeing a man covered in blood. "I went to him in shock, asking him, 'Are you OK?'" He says he saw injured and unconscious passengers being taken to the airport's first aid clinic.

"Some of them, I still don't know whether they were alive or not."

The experience left him shaken. "The threat is real," he tells me. "But I will not let the Houthis make me feel unsafe in my own country."

The airport attack was far from an isolated incident. BBC analysis of data from the US-based Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (Acled), a non-profit organisation, which collects data on political violence and protests around the world, identified 274 attacks on Saudi Arabia in almost five months between 1 July and 25 November.

According to Acled, most of these were intercepted, but at least 41 were not and in some cases debris from the interception also caused damage.

Drones featured in almost two-thirds of the attacks, while ballistic missiles were used in more than half, according to the data.

In the previous five months, Acled recorded just one Houthi attack on the country.

Backed by Iran, the Houthis have developed an increasingly sophisticated arsenal, dramatically extending their ability to repeatedly strike deep in Saudi territory.

For years, Houthi attacks were largely concentrated near the Yemeni border, with Riyadh targeted far less frequently. But since the collapse of the unofficial ceasefire, the Saudi capital, more than 700km (430 miles) away from the Yemeni border, is now coming under regular attack.

As well as the airport, oil installations and prominent buildings in the capital have been in danger.

Saudi Arabia has spent billions transforming its cities, attracting international investment and presenting itself to the world as a safe place to live, work and visit - the attacks have put this promise to the test.

Two prominent skyscrapers have been hit in Riyadh's financial district this month.

Saudi Arabia's tallest skyscraper, the PIF tower, was struck on 19 November

Eleven people were injured in a strike on the Public Investment Fund (PIF) Tower, which is the tallest in Saudi Arabia and is the headquarters of the country's sovereign wealth fund. The other was the Aramco building, home to the state oil company.

As we drove past the Aramco tower, the damage was a clear reminder of the threat facing the kingdom.

But within days, the building's exterior had been completely repaired, any visible sign of the attack erased. It was perhaps a reflection of Saudi Arabia's determination to project an image of stability and business as usual, even as the attacks continue.

The government has condemned "terrorist attacks targeting civilian and economic facilities" and said it would "take all necessary measures" to defend itself.

Even so, flights to the capital have been severely disrupted by the strikes, which have also targeted other locations, such as Medina and the airport in the eastern city of Dammam.

Many passengers travelling to Riyadh are being routed through different airports and making the final leg of the journey on land.

The flight we took to Dammam was almost empty. Riyadh's streets tell a different story, though.

Stallholders in Riyadh's markets are trading as normal

Restaurants are bustling, families browse at shopping centres and people go about their evenings seemingly undeterred by the threat overhead.

But getting people to speak openly about the conflict is difficult in a country where strict censorship laws and restrictions on freedom of expression make many wary of talking to the media.

Many of those who did speak to us expressed confidence in their country's ability to protect them. At a busy market, Badr says the airport attack was worrying, but life has quickly returned to normal. "I sleep comfortably," he says, praising the country's security forces.

Another man, Rashid, gestures towards the stalls around us: "The market is booming. People are buying and selling, going about their business. Everything is good."

But the normality he describes is periodically disturbed by a sudden buzz on the phone with an alert warning of an incoming attack. Then come the loud booms of air defences intercepting missiles and drones overhead.

We experienced one at 04:00 one morning, and the knowledge that not every attack is being intercepted can leave people afraid.

Alex Malouf says the attacks and alerts can be hard for children to deal with

British expatriate Alex Malouf, who has lived in Saudi Arabia on and off since 2006, says he worries about the psychological impact on his 11-year-old daughter, who has experienced security alerts while at school.

"There have been times when my daughter has said, 'Daddy, I'm scared.' It has been something which I think has shaken our reality."

Despite the attacks, Abu Khalil says he feels much safer in Saudi Arabia than at home in Yemen where fighting has intensified.

The Houthis' renewed offensive in western Yemen has seen the group capture territory along the Red Sea coast and threaten strategic routes towards the southern city of Aden, the government's temporary base.

The wreckage of a shoe factory following a Saudi-led strike on Sanaa on 17 November

The fighting has also intensified around Taiz , a government-controlled city that has endured years of siege and conflict.

Road closures resulting from the latest Houthi siege there have severely restricted deliveries of essential supplies, leaving more than 800,000 people cut off from humanitarian assistance, according to the UN children's agency Unicef. Food and fuel that can be found have shot up in price.

More than 360,000 people have been forced from their homes in Yemen since August, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM). And the UN Human Rights Office has verified 323 civilian casualties since then, including 76 killed, with children accounting for half of the dead.

A Saudi-led coalition of Arab states has responded to the Houthi advances and attacks on the kingdom with intensified air strikes, adding to the dangers faced by civilians. One strike in Sanaa earlier this month killed 44 people, according to Houthi authorities. Saudi Arabia says these operations were to protect the Yemeni population and global trade from the Houthis.

Saudi-led bombing campaigns during the earlier years of the war killed thousands of civilians and devastated homes, hospitals and schools.

The Houthis have also inflicted enormous suffering on civilians through shelling, missile and ground attacks on government-held territory, as well as repression in areas under their control.

Abu Khalil hopes that he will soon be able to bring his wife and children over to Saudi Arabia, away from the dangers in Sanaa, and says he "will not go back until the Houthis are gone".

Additional reporting by Jasmin Dyer and Ahmed Nour

MN202611_o80nxbtke5.t:
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi with Sheikh Hasina in Delhi in 2024 - Hasina was a close ally of India during her years in power

Sheikh Hasina has repeatedly vowed to return to Bangladesh.

Now the ousted prime minister has put a date on her homecoming - 16 December - and even outlined how she intends to make the journey.

The government in Dhaka, which had previously dismissed the prospect, is taking her latest declaration more seriously.

Hasina, 79, who fled to Delhi in August 2024 after a student-led uprising ended her 15-year rule, plans to go back on Victory Day, the anniversary of Bangladesh's triumph over Pakistan in the 1971 liberation war, her spokesperson said.

She was sentenced to death after being convicted of crimes against humanity for her role in the crackdown, in a trial held in her absence that raised questions about due process. Her Awami League party is banned in Bangladesh. The UN says as many as 1,400 people were killed by security forces during the uprising.

The government says she would be arrested immediately if she returned and has promised to carry out the death sentence.

Hasina now wants the Bangladesh government to arrange a flight from Delhi. If that fails, she could travel commercially or cross the land border.

"She is even prepared to walk into Bangladesh," Abu Obaidha Arin, a key aide to Hasina, told the BBC.

Sheikh Hasina fled to Delhi in August 2024 after a student-led uprising ended her 15-year rule

India and Bangladesh share a 4,096km (2,545 mile) border across five Indian states - West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. Her supporters, Arin said, had identified nine possible crossing points. "This is a carefully thought-out, precise plan. This is serious."

Dhaka has responded with defiance, insisting Hasina must be extradited.

"Reality and desire are different things," Humaiun Kobir, Bangladesh's state minister for foreign affairs, told reporters in Dhaka. "[The reality is] she's not a regular commercial passenger. She can only be brought back in handcuffs."

India's foreign ministry said on Wednesday that Hasina's extradition request was being examined through the "established process", adding that a voluntary return would be a separate matter.

Sheikh Hasina: The pro-democracy icon who became an autocrat

Hasina's conviction for crimes against humanity is testing India-Bangladesh ties

Many in Dhaka believe Hasina's declaration is more than a promise of homecoming.

They believe it is an attempt to test the government's authority, force her way back into the political conversation and exploit divisions among the parties that united to oust her. It also threatens to turn India's unresolved problem of sheltering a former ally into a more immediate diplomatic crisis.

The date is significant. Hasina is invoking Victory Day to reclaim her place in Bangladesh's founding narrative. Aides say she has spent months trying to keep her party alive in exile.

Tarique Rahman has yet to visit India, his neighbour, since becoming prime minister in February

Arin says Hasina has been in regular contact with party leaders and workers through interactive audio conversations on Telegram, keeping alive a network that might otherwise have been difficult to sustain from exile.

Over the past 18 months, he says, she has held more than 300 such meetings, reaching supporters across all 64 districts and the country's 300 constituencies. They are organised through the Awami League's 78 units and "can last four or five hours".

The meetings allow Hasina to listen directly to party workers, hear their grievances and understand what is happening on the ground, Arin says. He insists the response has been substantial and claims the party "could mobilise five million people to welcome her along the route from the border to Dhaka, forming a human chain".

"We have the organisational capacity to make that happen," he says.

That may be an ambitious claim. The Awami League remains a mass party with millions of supporters, but it is banned and largely shut out of mainstream politics. Much of its leadership is abroad, in jail or underground. Police have arrested supporters and filed thousands of cases against party workers.

Yet its supporters have continued to take to the streets, staging flash protests that have grown more frequent and confrontational in recent months.

Awami League supporters have staged flash protests across Bangladesh in recent months

Several districts have reported bomb attacks, arson and vandalism, though responsibility for some incidents remains disputed.

Gopalganj, Hasina's ancestral district, has proved particularly difficult for the authorities to control.

Awami League supporters have attacked police stations , external , torched vehicles and targeted homes and offices belonging to ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) leaders, reports say. Highways have been blocked , external with felled trees and burning tyres, bringing traffic to a standstill. In some areas, police have withdrawn , external amid fears of further attacks.

Supporters have staged 40 demonstrations and more than 140 riots up to 23 November, according to data from conflict monitoring group Acled (Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project). At least 11 people, including two civilians, have been killed in political violence this month, six directly linked to the unrest, the group says.

The party's ability to cause disruption, however, is not necessarily evidence of a broad resurgence.

Many in Dhaka remain sceptical that Hasina will actually return, viewing the announcement as a means of galvanising a demoralised party.

Yet the Awami League has achieved something politically: it is back in the conversation. Immediately after Hasina's fall, even mentioning the party was taboo. Now its future is being debated across the political spectrum.

Shafiqul Alam, editor of the English-language daily Daily Waadaa and former press secretary to the Muhammad Yunus-led interim government, believes the party is "exploiting cracks in the unity forged during the uprising".

He told the BBC that "disagreements" over the July Charter , external , proposed constitutional changes and the referendum have "widened divisions" between the elected BNP government and rivals Jamaat-e-Islami and the youth-led National Citizen Party (NCP).

Fire engulfs a police station in Gopalganj on 17 November amid unrest following the arrest of Awami League activists

"The Awami League sees an opening," Alam told the BBC. "The party believes this is an opportune moment to take to the streets, exploiting a weakened police force and divisions among the forces of the July uprising ."

Analysts say if Hasina returns it could just as easily deepen hostility as revive her party's fortunes. The government has framed the sporadic recent violence as terrorism, while supporters insist their demonstrations are peaceful and accuse the authorities of repression.

The larger question is whether Bangladesh can sustain the exclusion of a political constituency as substantial as the Awami League without creating another source of instability.

For India, the dilemma is increasingly difficult to manage.

Delhi has sheltered Hasina, but her public remarks have angered Dhaka, which wants her extradited. India has sought to repair ties through diplomatic outreach and talks on trade, border security and other bilateral issues, but relations remain strained.

The chill is striking: nearly 10 months into his tenure, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has yet to visit India.

NCP members stage a motorcycle rally in Dhaka on 24 November, protesting against violence allegedly carried out by the banned Awami League

A trip was reportedly in the offing in August, but Hasina's press conference in Delhi proved a setback to efforts to reset relations.

Avinash Paliwal, who teaches politics and international studies at SOAS University of London, argues that Hasina's latest announcement has "shifted the burden of choice to Dhaka rather than Delhi".

Delhi, he says, "feels it has tried its best" to work with Rahman's government over the past 10 months - "from appointing a political heavyweight as high commissioner , external with cabinet rank to offering fresh talks on security and trade".

"The failure of this outreach has left India disillusioned with Dhaka. India seems to have decided that bilateral relations will likely remain tense whatever it does, so there is little reason to stop Hasina from stirring the political pot."

Delhi has the leverage to restrain Hasina from making political statements on Indian soil, Paliwal argues, but may not want to exercise it.

Nor, in his view, is it in India's interest to see the Awami League permanently excluded from Bangladeshi politics.

Bangladesh security forces patrol and conduct drills in Dhaka's Shahbagh area on the Awami League's founding anniversary

"The political party still enjoys pockets of support across Bangladesh and is weaved into the social and political fabric of the country," he says. "So, yes, it is in India's interest, and also in Bangladesh's long-term interests, to rehabilitate the Awami League and take the path of political reconciliation."

That view is increasingly contested in Dhaka.

"There is a perception in Bangladesh that India wants to rehabilitate the Awami League. There are issues India has not resolved, including the extradition of Hasina. India has also not renewed the transit facilities that could benefit Bangladeshi garment exporters, while the Ganges water treaty , external is nearing expiry without much progress. But has India done enough to win back trust?" says Alam.

"For now, only tourist and medical visas have resumed. Everything else remains in limbo."

A Dhaka-based foreign-policy expert, who asked not to be named, says the two countries remain locked in "mutual frustration".

Vehicles pass a mural of Sheikh Hasina near Dhaka University

Hasina, he says, remains central to the impasse. "She remains the elephant in the room, but we also have to find a way to move beyond Hasina."

Paliwal argues that the least damaging outcome for India would be Hasina returning to face a fresh trial, with the Awami League rehabilitated under a different operational leadership.

"It will reintroduce a degree of balance in Bangladeshi politics, and will afford India space to protect its long-term interests and equities better," he says.

For now, 16 December is not yet a confirmed journey. But Hasina has already succeeded in making her return a question that neither Dhaka nor Delhi can ignore.

"December could be chaotic. Everyone in Dhaka is on edge," says the foreign-policy expert, warning of protests and confrontation as Hasina's proposed return date approaches - and the possibility that it could be postponed yet again.

"Hasina is unlikely to return, as she would face a death sentence. But her comments have clearly galvanized her supporters," says Pearl Pandya, Acled's South Asia analyst.

But the impasse is also complicating India's ties with Bangladesh. As Paliwal puts it, the "next window of serious negotiations will now open only after Hasina returns to Dhaka, or Dhaka relents under pressure and returns to the table".

Bangladesh's ex-PM Sheikh Hasina says she plans to return on 16 December

Violence erupts in Bangladesh as ousted PM's supporters stage protest

Why India wants Bangladesh's Tarique Rahman in Delhi

Rwanda is gearing up for the country’s First Endovascular Neurosurgeon, Taarifa Investigative Desk reliably reports.

Dr Sylvie Inyange is training from Addis Ababa, Ethiopia at the Habari Medical Plaza and Axon Stroke & Spine Center.

With the ambition to complete training as an endovascular neurosurgeon, Dr Inyange is getting support from Dr Wondwossen Tekle and Dr Akeza Teame.

Yvan Butera Rwanda’s State Minister in the Ministry of Heath visited Dr. Inyange at the Ethiopia based training facility.

“Dr Inyange will be able to treat strokes, brain aneurysms and other conditions affecting the blood vessels of the brain and spine. Using tiny catheters guided through the vessels, she will be able to remove clots and repair them without opening the skull,” State Minister Butera said on Friday.

MN202611_9xsb7kl7oe.t:
Ant McPartlin and Dec Donnelly present the show and host their own podcast

I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here host Declan Donnelly has said tensions between Mariella Frostrup and AJ Odudu over cooking duties on the show "became a much bigger deal than it should have".

Co-host Ant McPartlin said "cooking makes things very tense in camp", adding: "If they could zoom out a little bit in there, they'll realise it's not that deep. But they just can't, once they're in there".

Donnelly and McPartlin discussed on their podcast how relations became fractious, when Odudu attempted to help Frostrup cook on Saturday's episode - the next day Odudu was distressed after Frostrup accused her of being "aggressive".

On Wednesday 887 people complained to Ofcom about Sunday's episode in relation to "alleged bullying behaviour" by Frostrup towards Odudu.

Wayne Rooney tried to repair relations between AJ Odudu (left) and Mariella Frostrup on Sunday

Frostrup apologised during an amicable conversation on Tuesday, and Odudu accepted, explaining it was "triggering" because "it's a strong word to use in casual scenarios, particularly towards black women".

On their podcast, Hanging Out with Ant and Dec, Donnelly said tensions in camp started "surprisingly early".

"From day one cooking was tense and then it obviously came to a head with AJ and Mariella, and it spilled over to breakfast the next morning," he said.

McPartlin added: "You have 12 hungry mouths to feed and you and your sous chef, the other chef, are cooking and everyone is stood around looking at them. The pressure is quite a lot."

Donnelly continued: "When you are there, and so much of your life revolves around that mealtime, it's the only meal of the day you really get that isn't rice and beans.

"There is a lot of pressure and obviously Mariella was feeling that pressure.

"AJ wanted to come in and help and it all came to a head, and maybe because there was so much pressure and because it was so important, Mariella maybe didn't handle it very well around the campfire when she was cooking, and it spilled over into the next day - and it became a much bigger deal than it should have done."

He said the "most important thing" was that "the two ladies were able to sit down and drew a line under it, they were adult enough to sit there, talk it through, and move on together. If more people did that the world would be a much better place".

McPartlin agreed, saying: "If some of our leaders did that, the world would be a better place."

AJ Odudu said being called aggressive was "very harsh" and it was "an insane word" to use about her

On Wednesday, an Ofcom spokesperson told BBC News: "We are assessing the complaints against our rules, but are yet to decide whether or not to investigate."

On Thursday night, Frostrup completed her fourth bushtucker trial, which is voted for by the public.

Many viewers defended Odudu after the encounter.

They included broadcaster and comic Judi Love who said she felt "triggered by Frostrup's comment, while Britain's Got Talent judge and Strictly Come Dancing judge Motsi Mabuse also gave their support to Odudu.

BBC Radio 1 DJ Clara Amfo said: "Calling a black woman 'aggressive' when she is being anything else but is a classic microaggression."

Speaking on spin-off show I'm A Celebrity... Unpacked on Sunday, former campmate Jordan Banjo said Frostrup had handled the situation "poorly", but urged people to "give a bit of grace to Mariella, and everyone in the camp" because "you can't judge an abnormal situation by normal standards".

It is "a really weird situation that every single person's in, and I'm not sure if people go at stuff with the clearest head", he said, explaining: "You get these weird breakdowns, and I think that's what we're seeing."

Mariella Frostrup risked further tension when she told Odudu that "you don't take an apology well"

An ITV statement said: "The production monitors everyone in camp 24/7 and if at any time we feel someone has overstepped the line by using inappropriate language or displaying unacceptable behaviour, we would take steps to intervene and speak to everyone involved.

"The duty of care for our contestants is of the utmost importance to us. We take the welfare of the celebrities very seriously and have measures in place to ensure they are supported at every stage of the process: before, during and after filming."

MN202611_1j7qakni7z9.t:
Edward Iordandescu is the first Romanian to manage in the top four tiers of English football

New Watford boss Edward Iordanescu says he has inherited a "challenge" but also "an opportunity" as the club seeks to pull away from the Championship relegation zone.

The 48-year-old has replaced Alessio Dionisi, who was sacked on Sunday after only five months in charge, following a run of seven defeats in 10 league games.

Iordanescu became Watford's sixth new boss in less than 18 months and is the 25th manager since the Pozzo family took over the club in 2012.

He will take charge of the Hornets for the first time on Saturday when they travel to bottom club Derby County.

The Romanian met the media for the first time on Friday, and set out his vision for his tenure.

The Watford job is Iordanescu's first since leaving Legia Warsaw in October 2025, having won the Polish Super Cup with them last season.

It is the 10th managerial post of his 15-year coaching career, which has taken in Bulgarian club CSKA Sofia as well as Steaua Bucharest and Cluj - who he guided to the Romanian title and two domestic cups after joining midway through the 2020-21 season.

He also spent two and a half years in charge of Romania, guiding them to the last 16 of Euro 2024, where they were beaten by the Netherlands.

However, in his first job in English football, he inherits a Watford side three points above the drop zone and facing a fight for their second-tier status.

"I'm proud more than anything else and I'm honoured and happy to be here, but I'm also very aware of the challenge in front of me," Iordanescu told BBC Three Counties Radio.

"I don't want to make promises. I know the fans are not happy in this moment, but also I know that my words are not enough to bring them back, so they wait for facts. We need that, but of course there is a lot of work to do, there is a process in front of us and I hope we make the next steps right away.

"For me it's a challenge but at the same time it's an opportunity and I want to transform this opportunity into something good for the club, for the fans. This is the most important [thing]."

Prior to the dismissal of Dionisi, former Watford player Tom Ince - who left the club at the end of the 2025-26 season - told the BBC's 72+ Podcast there was "so much control away from the manager" at Vicarage Road.

While Ince, now at League Two side Tranmere Rovers, added his respect of positives of chairman Gino Pozzo's practises, he is not alone in speaking out about the board's influence.

Former England boss Sam Allardyce stated he turned down the Watford job in 2019 after claiming he was told how the side should play and which players should be in the XI.

But Iordandescu revealed that is not his expectation.

"I know my borders and I know my responsibilities." he said. "I'm in this club with a lot of quality people, professionals, people that know, understand, in detail, football, but starting yesterday I'm the number one in the technical side.

"I don't believe there's somebody here in the club that can overcome the coach, taking the technical knowledge, so it will be my responsibility, but also the technical part will be my decision all the time."

Pioneer or coach-eater? The complex world of Pozzo's Watford

From a purely statistical perspective, Watford's laboured start to the season under Dionisi could be credited to one key deficiency.

The Hornets have scored the fewest goals in the Championship, with only 13 in their 17 matches so far.

However, Iordanescu said his primary objective was not to thrill, but to win.

He said: "I always prefer to win 1-0 than 4-2. One-nil means you have an organised team, a team with some responsibility to engage 100% and to give everything for the result.

"So for me the priority is not to score more goals - [it is] to start to be organised, to start to act and react together on the pitch, to start to understand that the mindset should be a little bit different than what it was until now and to start to be efficient.

"In time we will see about scoring more goals, definitely every coach wants the team to score as much as possible."

Iordanescu also appeared to confirm he was in talks about taking over while Dionisi was still in charge.

It was reported on 12 November that the Hertfordshire club were in talks with him, but Dionisi, who had only been appointed in June, remained in charge across the international break and for Saturday's 4-0 defeat at Sheffield United.

The Italian was sacked on Sunday, with Iordanescu appointed on Wednesday.

Iordanescu said he had "asked for time" from the Watford hierachy before accepting the role.

He said: "I wanted to understand very clearly the objectives, the targets, so when I gave the final response, I was aware of everything.

"I'm here, I'm enthusiastic, I'm positive, I'm confident we can do good things together, and the thing which I count most on is the potential of this very young team. One of the youngest teams in the league."

But Iordanescu also took time to pay tribute to his predecessor.

"He [Dionisi] definitely worked hard," said Iordanescu.

"He did and left good things, very good things, already I saw many of them. But in football when things don't run the way you want and when the results are not backing up your work, it's difficult.

"I know he is a coach that put a lot of heart in his work and thank him for the good things that he did, and also tried to achieve here."

The task at hand now for Iordanescu is to succeed where Dionisi, and so many other Hornets bosses since their Premier League relegation in 2022, could not.

MN202611_qcptkbhqyx.t:
Manchester City have managed only five clean sheets this season

Manchester City 's leaky defence faces one of its most difficult tasks of the season with a trip to watertight Arsenal , aiming to put right their patchy recent form.

Enzo Maresca's side began the season with eight straight victories but have won only one of their past seven in all competitions inside 90 minutes and head to Emirates Stadium trailing the champions by six points even at this early juncture.

A Premier League defeat on Sunday could well have long-term consequences for City's title aspirations, with Mikel Arteta's men clearly standing above any other top-flight side as the ones to topple.

Though the Gunners dropped points last weekend with a draw at Newcastle , they continue to set the standards with a miserly defence that has conceded only seven goals in the club's opening 11 league games.

Asked why he felt City have dropped off in recent weeks, Maresca - who replaced Pep Guardiola as manager in the summer - said: "For me it's because we've had four months together. Transition requires time.

"It's probably because we won seven games in a row, with Champions League eight in a row. Everyone was thinking at City there's no transition but I've said many times I am not a magician. There is transition, it's normal.

"There are eight or nine new players, the manager is new so you need time and you can see different clubs when they had transition how complicated it is. For me, it's completely normal, I'm completely relaxed, no panic at all."

'Pass, pass, slow, slow' - Man City's slick machine grinding to a halt

Why Man City can't wear their new kit in Premier League

"We are conceding too many goals and we need to avoid that," was an obvious statement made by Maresca following last Saturday's 1-1 draw against Fulham.

City followed that up with another home stalemate against Napoli in the Champions League on Tuesday and have now conceded in 10 successive games in all competitions for the first time in seven years.

"[It was] far, far too easy to play through [City]," said former England captain Alan Shearer of Rodrigo Muniz's goal for Fulham on Match of the Day.

" Fulham 's throw-in was level with their own 18-yard box. For them to get through is not acceptable at any level, let alone when you are playing for Manchester City and Muniz ran past the entire midfield [to score]."

City have managed only five clean sheets all campaign, which is in stark contrast to Arsenal , who have kept double the amount so far, while Newcastle 's opening goal ended a run off 445 minutes without the ball hitting their net.

Maresca's men also have an issue by conceding the opener, having done so seven times in the past 10 games, and of the 14 goals they have shipped, six have come inside the first 20 minutes.

An early Arsenal goal may well be an important factor in deciding Sunday's contest.

Asked how his side can improve defensively, Maresca said: "Video [analysis], meetings, [on] pitch coaching, It is a mix of that.

"Some of the goals we concede we can avoid, so hopefully we can do that."

Man City fan questions what's behind Marc Guehi's recent struggles

The injury to key defender William Saliba has almost gone unnoticed for Arsenal as Ezri Konsa has stepped in to fill the void at centre-back seamlessly since joining from Aston Villa in the summer.

The England international has established a formidable partnership with Gabriel and the two have quickly formed an impressive understanding this season.

Maresca, meanwhile, admitted he was still "trying to find different" solutions to his team, which has been highlighted by the chopping and changing of his backline.

In 16 Premier League and Champions League games this season, the Italian has used eight different combinations in defence, which has given players little chance of fostering any sort of on-pitch relationships with each other.

City have also made seven errors leading to goals, compared to Arsenal 's one.

"You are concerned in some way because that is a lot of errors leading to goals," said former City defender Nedum Onuoha. "With some of the best players you ask, 'what are they really good at?' For some it is the fact they don't make mistakes.

"They are ruthless and relentless in the way they play but at this moment in time City are being punished for those errors.

"A manager can have the tactics and do the team talks, but if people are going to continue to make those mistakes, they will suffer."

The chant of "1-0 to the Arsenal " has been synonymous with the Gunners over the years and it could not be more apt under Arteta.

Since the start of last season, his side have won 16 matches in all competitions by that particular scoreline, compared to six by City.

After beating Sunderland in a chaotic match in September, Maresca said he would "prefer to win 1-0 than 5-3", suggesting his side needed more control and he re-iterated that message after the Fulham draw.

"Sometimes you need to win games 1-0 for a small difference and to keep a clean sheet but in this moment we are not able to do that," he admitted.

City, though, have scored five more league goals than Arsenal in this campaign and Sunday's hosts have injury concerns over goalkeeper David Raya.

The Spaniard is a doubt with the shoulder problem he picked up at Newcastle , and compatriot Kepa Arrizabalaga may deputise again as he did in the 1-1 draw against Borussia Dortmund in the Champions League on Tuesday.

City have fond memories of coming up against Arsenal 's stand-in keeper, after Kepa's howler for the opening goal contributed to their 2-0 Carabao Cup final triumph back in March.

A repeat result on Sunday will provide a much-needed morale boost for Maresca and his team.

MN202611_1t3nx4wfuji.t:
Falkirk and Rangers meet for a second time this season

The Scottish Premiership rolls into town again this weekend with crucial games in both halves of the table.

Last week, Falkirk beat St Johnstone to secure six top-flight wins in a row for the first time since 1966.

Victory at Ibrox on Saturday would make it seven in a row in the highest Scottish league for the first time since 1907, during a season in which the Bairns finished second.

In order to do that, John McGlynn's side would have to become the first Falkirk team to win against Rangers at Ibrox since a 1994 League Cup tie when Richard Cadette scored twice in a 2-1 victory.

Falkirk are also looking to hold on to third place, with Hearts a point behind having played a game fewer.

However, Rangers have their own motivation, not least extending their 14-match unbeaten run in all competitions - a sequence that has included 12 wins.

By winning their game in hand against Aberdeen on Tuesday, Rangers moved to within a point of Premiership leaders and reigning champions Celtic.

Therefore, three points would take Rangers top before Celtic visit Hearts on Sunday.

Two games in, Mario Frick's reign as Aberdeen head coach has produced 11 goals - six for, five against - and one win and one loss. Heavy metal football, as he promised.

Both were away from home - against Kilmarnock and Rangers - and on Saturday, Frick takes charge of a game at Pittodrie for the first time, with Dundee the visitors.

The Dons have won just twice at home in the Premiership this season, their last such victory coming in mid-October.

Dundee are still licking their wounds after last Saturday's 8-0 home defeat by Hearts and Tuesday's 2-1 loss away to Hibs.

Steven Pressley's side are on a three-match losing run after a promising start to the season.

Though they are not in any immediate danger of being dragged down towards the relegation zone, such a scenario may not be far away unless they arrest their current slide.

Four points separate St Johnstone in sixth and second bottom Motherwell.

Dundee are just below Saints on goal difference while three teams - Aberdeen, Hibernian and St Mirren - are a point above Well.

It's so tight and bottom side Kilmarnock, who visit St Mirren, are four points adrift and at risk of becoming detached.

This weekend's fixtures could make the order of the bottom seven look rather different come close of play on Saturday.

St Johnstone are away to fifth-placed Dundee United, but Aberdeen v Dundee, St Mirren v Kilmarnock and the evening meeting of Motherwell and Hibs at Fir Park pitch those congested sides up against one another.

'He's priceless for us' - O'Neill on match winner Duran

Celtic took only one point from last season's trips to Tynecastle but had the last laugh with victory over Hearts in Glasgow on the final day of the league season to tip Derek McInnes' side to the Premiership title.

McInnes' replacement Wouter Vrancken took his much-changed Hearts side to Celtic Park last month and were overrun in a 7-1 defeat, easily Celtic's best performance of the season so far.

Sunday is a chance for Hearts to atone for that loss and give Vrancken the sort of statement performance and win the home supporters are looking for.

Both sides had European fixtures on Thursday, with varying results.

Hearts were undone by a late goal in their 3-2 Conference League defeat at home to Monaco before Celtic boosted their hopes of Europa League progress with a 2-1 victory away to Portuguese side Torreense.

European hangovers notwithstanding, any goals would ensure an extension of no 0-0 draws between these sides since 2015.

MN202611_1krqsb9ippv.t:
Bruno Fernandes joined Manchester United in 2020

Manchester United have triggered their one-year option on captain Bruno Fernandes' contract.

The 32-year-old's deal was due to expire next summer but sources say both parties decided it was in their best interests to activate the option through to 2028.

It means overseas clubs will not be able to approach Fernandes when the transfer window opens on 1 January.

The Portugal international confirmed on Tuesday that discussions over a new contract had been paused. Sources say they will resume once United's league position has improved.

Fernandes has made 343 appearances for United, scoring 115 goals, since his £47m move from Sporting in January 2020.

Last season he broke the Premier League assists record and scooped all of the individual player of the year awards after an outstanding campaign as United finished third.

While there is doubt over his long-term future, extending the contract means United would be able to command a fee for Fernandes should he leave in the summer.

United had been open to selling Fernandes in the summer of 2025, with Saudi Pro-League club Al Hilal offering a huge deal.

After discussing the situation with his wife, Fernandes decided to stay, though he later said it "hurt" United were willing to sell him. He reiterated on Tuesday he was still ambitious to win the biggest honours in the game.

Fernandes is a doubt for Saturday's Premier League encounter with Brentford after returning from the Champions League trip to Sporting with a virus.

The playmaker, who scored both goals in the 2-2 draw with his former club, but did not train on Friday and head coach Mauricio Pochettino said he would take a decision on his captain's fitness on Saturday morning.

"We are going to assess during the day and then tomorrow see how he is when he wakes up," said Pochettino. "We are not going to take any risks."

MN202611_1txvanlo74f.t:
The prime minister's spokesperson has said broadcasters must "act responsibly" and that "we have no interest in hearing" what Huw Edwards has to say, following a backlash against new interviews with the disgraced former BBC News presenter.

Edwards, who was convicted in 2024 for making indecent images of children, has been interviewed for a Channel 4 documentary plus a podcast by the Observer and Tortoise Media.

"Our thoughts first and foremost will be with the victims of child sexual abuse and exploitation. We have no interest in hearing what he has to say," a Downing Street spokesperson said.

"There are extremely serious crimes and anyone convicted of them must face the consequences of their actions."

The No 10 spokesperson added that broadcasters "are expected to act responsibly and have appropriate regards to their audiences when making decisions".

Pressed on whether the prime minister believed Channel 4 had not acted responsibly, they said: "Channel 4 is editorially independent and decisions about individual programmes and contributors are a matter for them."

During the court case, Edwards admitted three counts of making indecent images of children. That involved having 41 images and videos, which were sent to him on WhatsApp – including some showing a victim aged between seven and nine.

Earlier, Environment Minister Emma Hardy said the plan by Channel 4 made her feel "sick", telling LBC , external it was giving a platform to "someone who is on the Sex Offenders Register".

"That platform doesn't exist for his child victims, does it?... It's not something I could support, and it's definitely not something I'd be watching."

Channel 4 has defended the programme, telling the BBC a "highly experienced director", Patrick Forbes, held Edwards to account with "no questions off limits, revealing his account of what led to his offending and very public downfall".

Conservative MP Dame Caroline Dinenage, chair of the House of Commons culture and media select committee, said the media outlets should "not just act as a platform" for Edwards to have a voice.

Any programme featuring him "needs to properly challenge his past actions" she said, along with raising "still unanswered questions" about whether Edwards will return more than £200,000 he was paid by the BBC , after he was first arrested.

The documentary and podcast will both be released on Tuesday, with some material expected to be published by the Observer on Sunday.

The interviews have also been criticised by three people who previously spoke to BBC News about allegations of Edwards' inappropriate behaviour.

One, who accused him in 2023 of sending them threatening messages, said it was "incredibly bizarre that anyone, big names like Channel Four, are platforming him when he's a convicted sex offender".

The person, who is anonymous and not connected to the criminal case, told BBC News on Thursday Edwards was "clearly trying to do a bit of damage repair" and they were "annoyed that he's being able to air these opinions".

Another person, who said Edwards sent them suggestive and "pushy" messages when they were working at the BBC, and was also not involved in the court case, said: "I'm pretty disgusted they are giving him the air time."

Additionally, a former junior BBC employee, who previously told BBC Newsnight's Victoria Derbyshire they had received inappropriate messages from Edwards, said "it seems a strange and irresponsible decision to give a platform to tell his story after the crimes he has been found guilty of.

"I hope that consideration has been given to his victims."

Duncan Craig, head of We Are Survivors, which supports male survivors of sexual abuse and rape, said it felt like the media companies were "not thinking about the victims in this particular case".

And it is the wrong time to release these programmes, coming during "a reckoning moment" for abuse in the media, he added.

"[It is] in fact giving somebody a platform that, in some way, shape or form, gives them the ability to nail themselves to the cross. That is not OK."

He added he does "fundamentally believe in rehabilitation" but that "this doesn't feel like it."

In a promotional clip released by the Observer, interviewer Ceri Thomas is seen saying he was "just deeply curious about how it was that a man of such prominence had got himself into this unbelievable, terrible fix".

"An 'unbelievable terrible fix' isn't somebody sat actively downloading 41 images of child sexual abuse, of which a number of them were at grade A level of of boys aged seven to nine being sexually abused," he said.

BBC broadcaster Nicky Campbell added , external his voice, saying: "I'm rather more concerned for the children in the photographs. What of their lives?"

The Observer, which is owned by Tortoise Media, has been asked for a response to the criticism.

Meanwhile, journalist Sangita Myska posted , external : "The rehabilitation [of] Huw Edwards' reputation via a 'personal journey' documentary is contemptible. He's a sex offender. What the hell is Channel 4 thinking?"

Fellow broadcaster Richard Bacon responded , external : "Why is that rehabilitation? It's a documentary. There are lots of them about lots of different people. About lots of different types of people."

MN202611_13bai6v3enp.t:
How New York reacted to postponement of Macy's parade

Touring musicians from across the US who descended on New York City to perform at the Macy's Thanksgiving parade have turned to fundraising to cover their costs, after getting stuck when the event was rearranged due to a storm.

A band from Texas told the BBC's US partner, CBS News, it had raised some $350,000 (£267,000) to pay for an extended stay for its 500 members. It saluted the kindness of its supporters.

A group of student musicians from Hawaii, meanwhile, voiced their relief after friends and family rallied around to cover their additional hotel, coach and meal costs.

The parade, a famous annual event, is now scheduled to take place on Saturday.

Earlier this week, organisers said they would it push back by two days, in part due to the concerns around flying giant inflatables in strong winds.

The balloons were temporarily deflated for a few days - and so too the spirits of those who had journeyed to the city to watch the action.

The move represented the first time the event had been postponed, although it was suspended altogether during World War Two.

Each year, a number of marching bands travel from across the country, some of them from high schools, to provide music for the event. This is considered a huge opportunity, as the parade is watched by millions of people in person and on TV.

Macy's postpones Thanksgiving parade due to severe weather

Hundreds of thousands still without power after storms hit US on Thanksgiving

The leader of the Texas band described his emotions as costs for his delegation were met.

"It's been exhausting and emotional to figure this out, but it has been incredibly humbling to see an outpouring of kindness," Ryan Demkovich, the director of the Pride of Pearland Marching Band at Pearland High School, near Houston, in Texas, told CBS.

Demkovich said contributions had arrived from businesses and individuals in the band's home community, with the help of a social media push.

The Pride of Pearland Marching Band from Texas - pictured rehearsing earlier this week - said it raised hundreds of thousands of dollars

Meanwhile, the Hawaii group, the the Nā Koa Aliʻi Hawaiʻi All-State Marching Band, said it would still be able to participate in the parade, as a result of the efforts of families, friends, and other supporters who raised more than $500,000.

Speaking to the BBC earlier on Thursday, the group's director Rickey H Badua described the time pressures. "We are racing to get this done," he explained.

The band is made up of hundreds of musicians from dozens of schools across the state. It had travelled almost 5,000 miles (8,000km) to get to New York.

"Getting the news that we got the parade postponed was not easy, and emotional, for our students," Badua said.

But the musicians sprang into action quickly, he said. "We come from a very far place," Badua said, adding that "to get so close to the finish line and not show up for it, we couldn't give up that easily".

The response from friends and family had been "incredible", he said.

New York City mayor on postponing 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade

Badua was hopeful his group would get the same experience he had when he first performed in the parade in 2003, as student drum major.

"The energy is palpable, people are just excited to see a band that is great."

Another musical act, from Illinois, told the BBC on Thursday it was trying to raise $175,000 to cover another night in a hotel, additional food, and bus costs back to the city of Champaign.

"Things are going well due to the very generous support of so many amazing human beings," said Prof Barry Houser, director of the University of Illinois Marching Illini.

While awaiting the parade, musicians and punters alike have sheltered from the heavy wind and rain that were brought by a storm to eastern areas of the US.

Hundreds of thousands of homes lost power, and coastal areas were flooded. The National Weather Service (NWS) expects conditions to improve gradually on Friday.

MN202611_6w4b45x7kz.t:
Canada's top court has largely upheld a Quebec law banning public sector workers from wearing religious symbols, including the hijab and the cross.

The law, known as Bill 21, faced legal challenges from a range of groups, including female Muslim, Sikh and Catholic teachers, who argued it violated their funadamental rights.

Quebec passed the law in 2019 under a unique fixture of Canada's constitution called the "notwithstanding clause" - a legal loophole that allows governments to override certain rights, like freedom of religion.

The Supreme Court's decision is one of the most closely-watched in Canadian history, with an impact that will be felt both in Quebec and across the country.

On Friday, the Supreme Court ruled that Quebec's use of the "notwithstanding clause" is valid, except for a section of Bill 21 that bars elected officials from wearing a face covering.

The court found that this provision of the law violates a section of the Canadian Charter protecting the democratic rights of all citizens, which is not covered by the notwithstanding clause.

Barring elected officials in Quebec's legislature from wearing a face covering would infringe on an individual's right to run for public office, the court found.

The court's majority also ruled that a Canadian court has the power to declare whether a law is consistent with the rights Charter even if the notwithstanding clause is invoked, but that they would not do so in this case.

MN202611_fi53jh12x7.t:
Slegers initially joined Arsenal in 2023 as an assistant coach under Jonas Eidevall

Arsenal have parted company with head coach Renee Slegers by mutual consent after a disappointing start to the season.

Slegers, 37, was initially appointed on an interim basis in October 2024 before being handed the role permanently three months later.

The Dutchwoman led Arsenal to a second Women's Champions League title in May 2025 and the inaugural Fifa Women's Champions Cup in February 2026.

But she leaves with the team sixth in the Women's Super League after 11 matches - 12 points behind leaders Chelsea.

Assistant coach Aaron D'Antino has also left the club, with assistant Melissa Clarke-Reed placed in interim charge as they begin the search for a permanent replacement.

D'Antino had been part of Arsenal's coaching staff since August 2018.

Arsenal director of women's football Clare Wheatley said the decision had been "extremely difficult".

"In leading us to glory in the Champions League and the inaugural Fifa Champions Cup, Renee has made a significant and lasting contribution to the history of Arsenal Football Club, with close support from Aaron," she said.

"After careful reflection, it is clear that results have been below the expected level, and change is necessary."

Chief executive Richard Garlick paid tribute to both departing coaches, describing Slegers as "a wonderful person" who had played "an integral role in some of the most historic achievements in the club's history".

"Our ambition is to compete for and win major trophies consistently, and our recent results have led us to conclude that a change is necessary to give us the best opportunity to achieve those goals," he added.

Macy's has postponed its 100th annual Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York because of severe weather. It is the first time the parade has been postponed due to weather.

Fans and volunteers voiced their disappointment over the postponement, with one remarking: 'We can't control the weather!'

Preparations to hold the iconic holiday celebration, known for its massive balloons that float among the city's skyscrapers, had already begun when the forecast for heavy rain and strong winds on Thursday led to the delay.

It is hoped the parade will take place on Saturday instead.

MN202611_vsgvvo9sci.t:
John Simpson: Ukraine is bowed but still unbroken as freezing weather sets in

Something weird happens when you reach Kyiv after the eight-hour drive from the Polish border: the clock on your mobile phone goes to midnight. It's not really for phones - it seems to be part of a wider strategy to disorient the missiles and drones the Russians are sending over.

Aside from little things like that, though, Kyiv seems fairly normal at first sight. You become well aware there's a war on when sirens begin to wail and people check their phones for the notifications which tell them there's a red alert and missiles are on their way. You can even buy gadgets that show you which direction the drones are coming from, and what type they are.

The drones and ballistic missiles have been hitting in sizeable numbers over the last couple of weeks. On the morning of Monday 16 November, the battle of the bridges began. Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge which links Russia to illegally occupied Crimea. Then it launched a bigger wave of missiles and drones, damaging the central road-bridge arch. A few hours later, presumably in revenge, Russia fired seven ballistic missiles at Kyiv, disabling two of the nine bridges that cross the River Dnipro.

The war has dragged on for more than four and a half years, killing what some estimate could be 100,000 Ukrainian troops and 18,000 Ukrainian civilians, according to the United Nations, and probably more. Its infrastructure, too, has been battered, as well as its morale. While temperatures drop to freezing at night, and with Ukrainians regularly suffering from no light, heat or water thanks to Russian strikes, can the country survive another difficult winter under bombardment? And what would a peace deal, if one could be struck, look like?

Kyiv is mostly dark at night, thanks to Russia's campaign of targeting Ukraine's electricity generating capability. In the blackness last week, the air raid sirens started wailing across the city, and our hotel's warning announcements came over the loudspeakers. Within a few minutes, we heard the first explosions. I jumped out of bed and stared out of the window into the darkness. After a few seconds two more missiles landed, lighting up the entire sky momentarily in a blaze of white and red. They were uncomfortably close.

Many people prefer to go to the shelters when there's a red alert. Others just stay in bed and hope the law of averages will protect them. It usually does. During one of the heaviest attacks last week, the number of fatalities was in single figures.

I went to the shelter in our hotel one night. The clearly audible thumps and crashes above ground, the permanent lighting, the snores and grunts of other people, and the attentions of the little biting flies that seem to thrive in the warm, crowded shelters made sleep hard.

Kyiv is entering its fourth winter following Russia's full-scale invasion

To the people who live here in Kyiv, it's frightening, certainly, if a drone or a missile hits close by, but enraging too. Over the years I've been in several cities that were being bombed by high-tech weaponry and the reaction always seems the same, whether it's Lebanon, Iraq, Serbia, or Ukraine: a combination of weariness and fury. In Kyiv the attacks come by night and day, making normal life almost impossible. An uninterrupted night's sleep is a rarity. The morning after the bridges were hit, people in the streets looked tired and worn.

Yet although they long for it to stop, there's no sign they want Ukraine to surrender. On the contrary, just about everyone I spoke to felt they had to keep fighting. That's borne out by an opinion poll last month by the KIIS organisation, a Ukrainian market research company, which found that 62% of people were prepared to put up with the war for as long as it took. Of those polled, 79% believed that Ukraine would win the war in the long run, and only 7% thought Russia would win. These aren't the reactions of a country which is being beaten to its knees.

I don't have any doubt that Ukraine can survive the winter. Food is plentiful, though prices are high. Water is a problem, because the regular attacks on the power grid mean that it can't be pumped with any regularity. Kyiv underwent a large transformation under the Soviets, so there are large numbers of high-rise blocks of flats everywhere. Labouring up and down the stairs when there's no power is daunting, especially when you've got to carry quantities of water home.

We came across a small crowd of people in their 20s who had gathered outside a nightclub for a rave at three in the afternoon, because of the 11pm curfew. "It's a way of getting a bit of respite from everything," said one young woman. "It makes me feel I can put up with everything," said a man.

Do people still support President Volodymyr Zelensky? My team and I met an elderly woman wandering around Independence Square in the centre of Kyiv holding a photo of her son, who was missing on the Eastern front. She blamed Zelensky; if he didn't insist on carrying on the war, she believed, her son would still be alive. It isn't a response most people seem to share. The same polling organisation, KIIS, found that Zelensky's trust ratings hover around 54% to 57% — way below the 90% he was registering in the early days of the war in 2022, but not too bad for a man who's been in power now for more than seven years.

Zelensky's ratings have dipped considerably

What comes across all the time in Kyiv is an absolute loathing of Russia. Putin reportedly launched his invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 because his intelligence chiefs assured him that Ukrainians longed to rejoin the Motherland.

Russian missiles have hit hospitals, clinics and schools. In many well-attested cases the Russians have used the "double-tap" method — sending in one missile, then waiting till the medics and rescuers gather before sending in another. At least 20,000 Ukrainian children have been abducted and taken to Russia, according to Ukraine's Ministry of Justice. In late March 2022, when the Ukrainians recaptured the satellite town of Bucha, on the outskirts of Kyiv, they found shocking evidence of torture and murder. Ukrainian soldiers call their Russian enemies Orcs, after the sub-human brutes in The Lord of the Rings. A country that has endured this kind of thing doesn't quickly forgive and forget. Russia denies that it targets civilians or civilian infrastructure.

Ukraine has never lost its own identity, even during the Soviet period. Some of Ukraine's culture was absorbed by Russia — "They call borsch [a famously delicious soup made of beetroot] theirs, but they got it from us," a waiter in a café here told me proudly. After the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, Ukraine overwhelmingly voted for independence. The war has brought a fierce renewal of this desire to be completely separated from Russia.

It's not my usual beat, but my team and I went to film on the set of MasterChef Ukraine, currently one of the country's favourite television programmes. The studio was borrowed; the original one had been bombed. The executive producer had his phone in his hand the whole time, and was constantly glancing at it. The moment a red alert showed, it was his duty to shepherd everyone off the set to a nearby shelter. "People see our cuisine as a way of expressing their national identity," he said. It's one of the reasons the programme is so popular.

There are other ways in which people express their Ukrainian national identity under the bombs. There has been a boom for books being written and published about Ukraine and Ukrainian identity. Ukrainian and Russian are close as languages, though vocabulary and pronunciation differ. Nowadays the differences are emphasised. "Woe betide a writer who uses Russian spellings," a Ukrainian novelist told me.

The war will end at some point; wars always do. But there has to be a clear winner before anyone backs down, and a lasting peace can be negotiated. US President Donald Trump and his advisers, people like Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, with their business backgrounds, have approached the situation as though it's a form of mergers and acquisitions: make a deal attractive enough, and the other side will accept it.

So, last week, Washington was rumoured to be offering a very Trumpian deal, that Ukraine should accept the loss of the land in the east which the Russians now control, and in return it was rumoured it could join Nato. It was a non-starter, because Russia would never accept it. The sweetener, in this US plan, was that the West's sanctions against Russia would be lifted, and both sides would benefit from unrestricted trading once again.

But neither side sees this as being about trade and profit. For Russia, it's about the dangers of being humiliated if it doesn't win. President Vladimir Putin has made it his personal war. By illegally taking Crimea from Ukraine in 2014, he made himself very popular in Russia. If he doesn't win this second stage of a 12-year campaign against Ukraine, the consequences for him personally could be disastrous. He's already had to face down one attempt against his rule: his former associate Yevgeny Prigozhin's march on Moscow in June 2023. In a much-quoted remark, reported last August, Putin is said to have confided to his associates that if he didn't win the war "they'll hang me". My sense is he's not concerned about trade with the West and the profit that will bring, so much as about his personal survival.

Similarly, Ukrainians aren't interested in the precise details that have leaked out of the various negotiations between the Americans and Russians. Their contempt for the US is immense; "they just failed us," said one Ukrainian I spoke to.

And they don't believe Russia will stick to any future peace agreement anyway. "They signed a treaty to accept our borders, and Putin broke it," a young man told me as he sat hunched over his laptop in a bookshop. "The only solution is to defeat them."

Tens of thousands of soldiers have died since the outbreak of war

Other people talked about the need to get huge reparations from Russia for the terrible destruction it has visited on their country. According to one estimate, reconstruction and recovery will cost more than $500bn (£383bn), an unthinkably huge amount for a country whose GDP was $200bn before the war. President Trump and his advisers don't seem to have addressed any of these issues in their negotiations.

Here in Kyiv, peace doesn't seem at all close. Russia's efforts to make life intolerable for Ukraine's citizens are certainly having a major effect. The war is often frightening for ordinary people, and it can be appallingly destructive of property and lives. But short of hugely escalating by attacking Ukraine with nuclear weapons, which is something China and the US are both thought to have warned him not to do, Putin can't seem to strike the knock-out blow against Ukraine that he needs.

At present it seems to people in Ukraine that the war will never come to an end. Yet it will, at some point: and then the crucial requirement will be to work out ways to stop Russia coming back for another round. One way would be if Ukraine joins Nato, but that's something Russia would only accept if it had been comprehensively defeated. Ukrainians might think that can happen, but most Western onlookers are more sceptical.

The daily and nightly sirens, the explosions of missiles and drones, the shortages and the fear and the darkness are all terrible. But they aren't enough to destroy Ukraine's will to continue fighting.
